'''Jerry Lee Rice''' (born October 13, 1962)<ref name="Pro-Football-Ref-1" /> is an American former professional [[American football|football]] [[wide receiver]] who played for 20 seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He won three [[Super Bowl]] titles with the [[San Francisco 49ers]] before two shorter stints at the end of his career with the [[Oakland Raiders]] and [[Seattle Seahawks]]. For his accomplishments and numerous records, Rice is widely regarded as the greatest wide receiver of all time and one of the greatest players in NFL history.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/columns/story?columnist=sando_mike&id=3309223 |title=Start with Rice No. 1, Moss No. 2 in best WR debate |last=Sando |first=Mike |date=March 26, 2008 |website=[[ESPN.com]] |access-date=December 27, 2019 |archive-date=January 9, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160109091556/http://sports.espn.go.com/nfl/columns/story?columnist=sando_mike&id=3309223 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.espn.com/blog/nfcwest/post/_/id/13874/the-case-for-rice-as-the-greatest-ever |title=The case for Rice as the greatest ever |last=Sando |first=Mike |date=February 4, 2010 |website=[[ESPN.com]] |access-date=December 27, 2019 |archive-date=December 27, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191227140012/https://www.espn.com/blog/nfcwest/post/_/id/13874/the-case-for-rice-as-the-greatest-ever |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.nflcdn.com/halloffame/story/0ap1000000221587/article/joe-montana-jim-brown-on-hall-of-fame-50th-anniversary-team |title=Joe Montana, Jim Brown on Hall of Fame 50th Anniversary Team |last=Harrison |first=Elliot |date=July 29, 2013 |website=NFL.com |access-date=February 21, 2017 |quote=Considered by many ... to be the NFL's greatest player |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171201185923/http://www.nflcdn.com/halloffame/story/0ap1000000221587/article/joe-montana-jim-brown-on-hall-of-fame-50th-anniversary-team |archive-date=December 1, 2017 |url-status=dead }}</ref> His biography on the official [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] website names him "the most prolific wide receiver in NFL history with staggering career totals".<ref name="pfhof">{{Cite web |title=Jerry Rice |url=https://www.profootballhof.com/players/jerry-rice/ |access-date=June 3, 2022 |website=Pro Football Hall of Fame Official Site |language=en |archive-date=May 19, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220519235825/https://www.profootballhof.com/players/jerry-rice |url-status=live }}</ref> In 1999, ''[[Sporting News|The Sporting News]]'' listed Rice second behind [[Jim Brown]] on its list of "Football's 100 Greatest Players".<ref name="SN100">{{Cite news |last=Matthews |first=Bob |date=August 15, 1999 |title=Sporting News Top 100 Football Players |page=3D |work=Democrat and Chronicle |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/4376402/sporting_news_top_100_football_players/ |url-status=live |access-date=February 27, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181116023025/https://www.newspapers.com/clip/4376402/sporting_news_top_100_football_players/ |archive-date=November 16, 2018 |via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> In 2010, he was chosen by [[NFL Network]]'s [[NFL Films]] production ''[[The Top 100: NFL's Greatest Players]]'' as the greatest player in NFL history.<ref name="Barall-2010" />

Rice played [[college football]] for four seasons with the [[Mississippi Valley State Delta Devils football|Mississippi Valley State Delta Devils]], setting several [[National Collegiate Athletic Association]] (NCAA) and team receiving records, including becoming the all-time leader in NCAA receiving touchdowns. He joined the 49ers after being selected with the 16th overall pick of the [[1985 NFL draft]]. After a modest rookie season, Rice emerged in the following season as one of the best receivers in the league, leading the NFL in receiving yards and touchdowns, a feat he achieved six times. In 1987, Rice set the record for most receiving touchdowns in a season, with 22, in a twelve-game strike-shortened season. He won back-to-back championships in [[Super Bowl XXIII|1988]] and [[Super Bowl XXIV|1989]], and was the MVP of the former championship. Rice developed connections with quarterbacks [[Joe Montana]] and [[Steve Young]] that are viewed as among the best in NFL history, helping him lead the league in both receiving yards and touchdowns six times, and in receptions twice.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Santorsa |first=Tony |date=December 7, 2011 |title=NFL History: Top 50 QB-WR Tandems of All-Time |url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/972343-top-50-qb-wr-tandems-in-nfl-history |access-date=June 3, 2022 |website=Bleacher Report |language=en |archive-date=June 3, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220603183939/https://bleacherreport.com/articles/972343-top-50-qb-wr-tandems-in-nfl-history |url-status=live }}</ref>

Going into the 1990s, Rice won a third Super Bowl in [[Super Bowl XXIX|1994]], and a second Offensive Player of the Year Award. After recovering from a knee injury and his play regressing, San Francisco released him in June 2001, where the Raiders would sign him to a four-year deal. He continued to start for the team, and helped lead them to an appearance in [[Super Bowl XXXVII]], where they were defeated by the [[2002 Tampa Bay Buccaneers season|Tampa Bay Buccaneers]], affecting Rice's previously unblemished Super Bowl record. Midway through 2004, the Raiders traded him to the Seahawks, where he spent his final season.<ref>{{Cite web |date=October 19, 2004 |title=Raiders agree: Rice to Seattle |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=1904779 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180626191129/http://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=1904779 |archive-date=June 26, 2018 |access-date=August 13, 2022 |website=[[ESPN.com]] |language=en |agency=[[Associated Press]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Cour |first=Jim |date=October 20, 2004 |title=Rice's trade to Seahawks reunites star wide receiver with Holmgren |url=https://www.spokesman.com/stories/2004/oct/20/rices-trade-to-seahawks-reunites-star-wide/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220814011946/https://www.spokesman.com/stories/2004/oct/20/rices-trade-to-seahawks-reunites-star-wide/ |archive-date=August 14, 2022 |access-date=August 13, 2022 |website=The Spokesman-Review |agency=[[Associated Press]]}}</ref> He briefly signed with the Broncos, retiring shortly before the start of the 2005 regular season.

Rice is the career leader in most major statistical categories for wide receivers,<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.nfl.com/history/randf/records/indiv/receiving |title=Individual Records: Receiving |website=NFL.com |access-date=April 24, 2011 |archive-date=October 15, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181015205829/http://www.nfl.com/history/randf/records/indiv/receiving |url-status=live }}</ref> including [[Reception (American football)|reception]]s, receiving [[touchdown]]s, receiving yards, scrimmage yards, and total touchdowns, holding the postseason records for these statistics, and once held the single-season records for yards and touchdowns. He scored more points than any other non-[[Placekicker|kicker]] in NFL history with 1,256.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/leaders/scoring_career.htm |title=NFL Points Scored Career Leaders |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en |access-date=October 29, 2018 |archive-date=November 25, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181125132126/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/leaders/scoring_career.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> Rice was selected to the [[Pro Bowl]] 13 times (1986–1996, 1998, 2002) and named All-Pro twelve times in his 20 NFL seasons, including ten First-team All-Pros, tied for the most by any player. Rice was inducted into the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] in 2010 and the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] in 2006. Rice was inducted into the [[Mississippi Sports Hall of Fame]] in 2007, and in the same year was inducted into the [[Bay Area Sports Hall of Fame]]. The NFL honored him as a member of the [[NFL 1980s All-Decade Team]] and the [[NFL 1990s All-Decade Team]], as well as both the [[NFL 75th Anniversary All-Time Team]] and [[NFL 100th Anniversary All-Time Team]].

'''Jerry Lee Tagge''' (born April 12, 1950) is an American former professional [[gridiron football|football]] player who was a [[quarterback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL), [[World Football League]] (WFL) and [[Canadian Football League]] (CFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Nebraska Cornhuskers football|Nebraska Cornhuskers]], leading them to consecutive [[College football national championships in NCAA Division I FBS|national championships]] in 1970 and 1971.   Tagge played professionally with the [[Green Bay Packers]] of the NFL from 1972 to 1974, the [[San Antonio Wings]] of the WFL in 1975, and the [[BC Lions]] of the CFL from 1977 to 1979.

'''Jesse Lewis Baker''' (July 10, 1957 – January 16, 1999) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive end]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Houston Oilers]] and the [[Dallas Cowboys]].

Baker played [[high school football]] for the [[Rockdale County High School]] Bulldogs in [[Conyers, Georgia]] in 1973 and 1974, where he earned all-state first-team honors both years. He was also a stand-out in track and field. He played [[college football]] at [[Jacksonville State University]] (JSU); while he was there, he was defensive MVP of the [[1977 Grantland Rice Bowl]], and was inducted to the JSU Hall of Fame in 1989.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://jsugamecocksports.com/hof.aspx?hof=15&path=&kiosk=|title=Jesse Baker (1989) - Hall of Fame|website=Jacksonville State University Athletics}}</ref> Baker was selected in the second round of the [[1979 NFL draft]].

Baker played nine seasons in the NFL with the Oilers.  He recorded 15.5 quarterback sacks and returned a fumble for a touchdown in his rookie season in 1979, despite starting only two of 16 games.  He recorded 6.5 sacks in 1980 and 10 more in 1981 as a part-timer before becoming a starter in the strike shortened 1982 season.  Baker started 57 consecutive games and recorded 29.5 more sacks.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/B/BakeJe21.htm | title=Jesse Baker Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College | website=[[Pro-Football-Reference.com]] }}</ref>
He died from an enlarged heart when he was 41.

'''Jerry Edward Meyers''' (February 21, 1954 – November 16, 2007) was an American professional [[American football|football]] [[defensive tackle]] who played for the [[Chicago Bears]] and the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] at [[Northern Illinois University]].<ref name="auto1">{{Cite web |title=Jerry Meyers stats |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/M/MeyeJe20.htm |access-date=December 15, 2023 |publisher=Pro Football Reference}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Jerry Meyers, DT |url=https://www.nfl.com/players/jerry-meyers/ |access-date=December 15, 2023 |work=NFL}}</ref>

Meyers grew up in [[Chicago]], Illinois, and attended [[Lake View High School (Chicago, Illinois)|Lake View High School]] where he was selected all-division in 1970.<ref name="auto">{{Cite web|url=https://niuhuskies.com/news/2007/11/20/Services_Set_Tuesday_for_Ex_Northern_Illinois_Chicago_Bears_Defensive_Lineman_Jerry_Meyers|publisher=[[Northern Illinois Huskies]]|title=Services Set Tuesday for Ex-Northern Illinois, Chicago Bears Defensive Lineman Jerry Meyers|date=November 20, 2007}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-daily-chronicle/136863726/|newspaper=[[The Daily Chronicle (Illinois)|The Daily Chronicle]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=July 19, 1978|page=13|title=A new Jerry Meyer visits DeKalb|author=Enlund, Tom}} {{Open access}}</ref> He played [[college football]] for the [[Northern Illinois Huskies football|Northern Illinois Huskies]] and was a three-year [[Varsity letter|letterman]], being a team [[Captain (sports)|captain]] as a [[Senior (education)|senior]] and ending his college career with 269 [[Tackle (football move)|tackles]].<ref name="auto"/> He was later inducted into the Northern Illinois Hall of Fame and was chosen to the school's All-Century team in 2000.<ref name="auto"/>

Meyers, selected by his hometown Chicago Bears in the 15th round of the [[1976 NFL draft]], survived being released numerous times to play four seasons and 47 games with the team.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.profootballarchives.com/playerm/meye02000.html|website=Pro Football Archives|title=Jerry Meyers Stats|access-date=December 15, 2023|archive-date=December 15, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231215190626/https://www.profootballarchives.com/playerm/meye02000.html|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.profootballarchives.com/transactionsm/meye02000.html|website=Pro Football Archives|title=Jerry Meyers NFL Transactions|access-date=December 15, 2023|archive-date=December 15, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231215190626/https://www.profootballarchives.com/transactionsm/meye02000.html|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-daily-chronicle/136863575/|newspaper=[[The Daily Chronicle (Illinois)|The Daily Chronicle]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=October 27, 1979|page=7|title=Bears' Meyers knows battle for survival|author=Armstrong, Rick}} {{Open access}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-journal-times/136863638/|newspaper=[[The Journal Times]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=September 9, 1979|page=25, [https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-journal-times/136863700/ 29]|title=He can't 'Bear' mind games|author=Eickhorst, Mark}} {{Open access}}</ref> He recorded one [[fumble]] recovery and unofficially made 5.5 [[Quarterback sack|sacks]] with the Bears, later playing two games with the Kansas City Chiefs in 1980 before retiring.<ref name="auto1"/> He had a brief stint with the [[Chicago Blitz]] of the [[United States Football League]] (USFL) in {{USFL Year|1983}} but did not appear in any games.<ref name="auto"/>

Meyers died on November 16, 2007, at the age of 53.<ref name="auto"/>
